demographics.trauma_type: Unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one

Triggers.value: Talk about people loosing loved ones

Threat.value: I find it harder to feel safe at night than during the day
My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger
I feel on guard even inside my own home

Memory.value: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory
When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief
My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images.

Negative Appraisals.value: I feel like I don't know myself anymore
I feel isolated and set apart from others
My life has been destroyed by the trauma

issues.item: Pain Recall: When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event
issues.explanation: Physical pain in the same body parts as during the event is hard to reconcile with the indexed trauma being an unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one, unless the patient was also physically injured during the event. That makes this item clinically implausible from the provided trauma context.

A global mistrust appraisal is a weak fit with bereavement trauma unless there is some interpersonal betrayal, negligence, or assault-related context. The rest of the profile centers on loss, alarm, and isolation rather than interpersonal threat from other people, so this item is not well supported by the trauma type or the other selected items.

For trauma involving the unexpected death of a loved one, ambulances can plausibly cue the death context and workplace cues may be idiosyncratically linked, but 'People cycling' is hard to connect clinically unless the loved one died in a cycling-related incident, which is not reflected anywhere else in threat, appraisals, or memory. It stands out as a trigger with no supporting context in the rest of the profile.

issues.item: Memory: Shame on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense shame
issues.explanation: The memory profile is dominated by grief-related recall and affective reliving without clear imagery, which fits bereavement trauma. 'Intense shame' on recall is not impossible, but here it lacks support from the negative appraisals, which focus on identity loss, isolation, and life destruction rather than self-blame, guilt, or humiliation. In this profile, shame is insufficiently integrated with the rest of the formulation and trauma type.

vignette:
Raymond Okafor was a 55-year-old African American man who came to treatment several months after his wife died suddenly, leaving him with a PCL-5 score of 67 and a life that, in his words, no longer felt like his own. The death had been unexpected and traumatic: one evening she had collapsed at home, and by the time the ambulance arrived there was nothing anyone could do. Raymond could still picture the blur of that night in pieces - the hallway light, the stretcher, the flashing emergency lights outside the house - but just as often he was hit by the raw feeling of it without a clear picture at all, a surge of panic and grief that seemed to rise out of nowhere. From the start, ambulance sirens, talk of other people losing loved ones, and even the sight of the workplace where he painted houses were enough to pull him back toward that night. A passing ambulance on the street could make his chest tighten and his thoughts race to his wife; a conversation at work about someone's mother or brother dying could leave him staring blankly at a wall, overwhelmed by the same grief he felt when he first heard she was gone. Each of those cues did more than upset him: they instantly felt like danger, as if something terrible were about to happen again. The siren on a city street or the sound of a service vehicle arriving at a job site could put him on edge before he had time to think, and the scene at work itself - the noise, the trucks, the talk of emergencies - became a place where threat seemed to follow him in. He noticed that remembering the event was rarely a calm recollection. The memories came as vivid images - his wife on the floor, the paramedics kneeling beside her, the look on the faces of neighbors gathered outside - and once those images surfaced, he felt emotionally flooded and then immediately on guard, as if danger were still unfolding in front of him. When those pictures broke through, they did not stay in the past; they pulled him straight back into the room, with the hallway light, the stretcher, and the flashing lights feeling close enough to touch. Afterward, even ordinary sounds and sights around him seemed to carry the same charge, as if the memory had trained him to see warnings everywhere.

Over time Raymond came to believe that the trauma had not simply taken his wife but had taken something essential from him as well. He said he did not know himself anymore and felt set apart from other people, especially when coworkers joked about family or spoke casually about the future. Once he had settled on that meaning, almost anything could confirm it: a passing ambulance, a question about someone being sick, or even hearing a neighbor mention a funeral would land as proof that the world was unsafe and that he was permanently changed by it. Those appraisals made him feel as though danger was already in the air around him, before anything had actually happened. That sense that his life had been destroyed sat heavily with him and made ordinary moments feel contaminated by loss. It also sharpened his vigilance. At night, when the house was quiet and his wife's absence was most obvious, he found it harder to feel safe than during the day; he lay awake listening for sounds from outside, body tense and ready to react, and even inside his own home he felt on guard. He noticed that the more he told himself he was broken and isolated, the more his body stayed braced for danger, as if his mind were warning him that something terrible could happen again at any moment. Those beliefs fed back into the memories too. Having decided that he was damaged beyond repair, he walked through his days already expecting threat, so new cues stood out sharply and caught hold of him. That same conviction also kept pulling him back to the night his wife died, making the images return with a force that seemed to prove his fear about himself. When he tried to think about his wife, the pictures came quickly, but they were often followed by a blank, unbearable emotional wave that confirmed for him that the loss had shattered him. In those moments he would be flooded with the conviction that his life had been ruined beyond repair. Each time the memory returned, it left him feeling as if the danger were still present, not over and done with, and that immediate sense of threat made the pictures harder to shake. The same intrusion also led him straight back to the thought that he was broken by it and would never be the same man he had been before.

Raymond also began to manage his distress by avoiding the places and topics that set it off, though the relief never lasted. He started taking different routes to avoid ambulances whenever possible and found himself pulling away from conversations at work that turned to illness, funerals, or other people's bereavements. The more he had come to see the world as dangerous and himself as unable to cope, the more even small things started to register as warnings - an ambulance heard two blocks away, a remark about a hospital, a neighbor's car with the lights still on late at night. Those cues kept him scanning, and the scanning made it feel as though threat was always just beneath the surface. At his painting job, which should have kept him busy, he became uneasy around the rhythm of the workplace itself - the noise of engines, the sight of service vehicles pulling up near a site, even the mention of a colleague being late because of an emergency. Each of these moments could spark the same chain: the trigger would bring back the images or the emotional force of his wife's death, the memories would make him feel exposed and unsafe, and the feeling of being changed and alone would push him to keep his distance from people and places that might remind him of what happened. He gradually spent less time chatting with coworkers and more time working in silence, which only deepened the sense that he was apart from others.

By the time he sought help, Raymond was sleeping poorly, checking the doors at night, and feeling constantly keyed up in a way that made him exhausted and irritable. He described moving through his days with the sense that the world could break open without warning, and that anything connected to ambulances, his work, or stories of loss could drag him back into the most painful parts of that night. Even when he was trying to keep busy, the persistent sense of danger kept the memory close, so a siren heard from inside the house or a vehicle pulling up outside his painting job could bring the whole scene back in a flash. Once that happened, the old fear returned with it, making the cue feel even more powerful and harder for him to dismiss the next time. What brought him in was the fear that he was becoming unreachable even to himself, and what he most hoped for was some way to feel safe in his own home again without being ambushed by the pictures, the grief, and the certainty that his life had ended when his wife died.

violations.explanation: The vignette shows triggers leading to distress, but does not explicitly state that triggers cause a sense of threat.
The vignette links triggers to vivid memories and emotional reactions, but does not clearly state that triggers drive the trauma memory itself.
The vignette shows triggers prompting distress and reminders of the loss, but does not clearly state that triggers lead to negative appraisals.
The vignette describes negative beliefs increasing vigilance, but does not explicitly state that those appraisals produce threat as a causal effect within one paragraph.
The vignette says beliefs feed back into the memories, but does not clearly state that negative appraisals generate the memory content or intrusion.
The vignette does not explicitly show negative appraisals causing triggers or cue reactivity.
The vignette shows memories making him feel flooded and on guard, but does not clearly state that the memory causes threat as a causal relationship within one paragraph.
The vignette says memories are followed by a conviction that his life was ruined, but does not clearly state that the memory leads to negative appraisals in causal form.
The vignette does not clearly state that memories themselves generate triggers.
The vignette says feeling threatened increases guarding, but does not clearly state that threat drives the memory/intrusion process.
The vignette shows feeling unsafe and on guard, but does not clearly state that threat causes triggers to become activated.

vignette_attempts.feedback:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Triggers → Threat: The vignette shows triggers leading to distress, but does not explicitly state that triggers cause a sense of threat.
  e.g. "The cues led to a feeling of danger that felt as real as the original event."
  e.g. "A knock at the door after dark sent her heart into her throat — her body read it as an emergency, even when her mind knew better."
  e.g. "Sitting in the waiting room, she noticed a man watching her from across the room and felt the same cold certainty: something terrible was about to happen."
- Triggers → Memory: The vignette links triggers to vivid memories and emotional reactions, but does not clearly state that triggers drive the trauma memory itself.
  e.g. "The smell of his cologne in the lift sent the whole night flooding back before she had even reached her floor."
  e.g. "Hearing that song on the radio dragged her straight back into the room where it happened, as if no time had passed at all."
  e.g. "Walking past the bus stop where it occurred, she was no longer on the street — she was back there, every detail sharp and close."
- Triggers → Negative Appraisals: The vignette shows triggers prompting distress and reminders of the loss, but does not clearly state that triggers lead to negative appraisals.
  e.g. "Every time she walked through that car park, the thought arrived with her: this is what your life is now — flinching at nothing."
  e.g. "Seeing a man in the same jacket made her think, with quiet certainty, that she would never stop being afraid."
  e.g. "The sound of raised voices next door told her, with a logic she couldn't argue with, that nowhere was ever really safe."
- Negative Appraisals → Threat: The vignette describes negative beliefs increasing vigilance, but does not explicitly state that those appraisals produce threat as a causal effect within one paragraph.
  e.g. "Having decided that she was permanently vulnerable, she walked into rooms already braced — the threat arrived with her before anything had happened."
  e.g. "The belief that she was a target — not unlucky, but chosen — meant that every unfamiliar face carried a weight of potential danger."
  e.g. "Her certainty that she couldn't protect herself made every new situation feel like a test she was already failing."
- Negative Appraisals → Memory: The vignette says beliefs feed back into the memories, but does not clearly state that negative appraisals generate the memory content or intrusion.
  e.g. "The belief that she was permanently changed kept bringing her back to the moment it had happened, as if she needed to locate exactly where she had been lost."
  e.g. "Telling herself that she should have seen it coming made the memory more vivid and easier to find — it sat there waiting, proof of her failure."
  e.g. "The conviction that she was weak fed directly into the flashback, colouring it, making it worse: she wasn't just there again, she was there again and helpless."
- Negative Appraisals → Triggers: The vignette does not explicitly show negative appraisals causing triggers or cue reactivity.
  e.g. "Once she had concluded that the world was fundamentally unsafe, almost anything could confirm it — a figure in her periphery, the wrong tone of voice, footsteps behind her."
  e.g. "The belief that she couldn't trust her own judgement meant that things she would once have registered and dismissed now snagged and held her attention."
  e.g. "Her conviction that it would happen again meant she moved through ordinary days as if they were mined — every ambiguity became a potential signal."
- Memory → Threat: The vignette shows memories making him feel flooded and on guard, but does not clearly state that the memory causes threat as a causal relationship within one paragraph.
  e.g. "Once the memory had surfaced, she couldn't shake the sense that the danger was still present — that it had simply moved into her body rather than gone away."
  e.g. "The flashback left her standing in her own kitchen feeling hunted, even with the door locked and the lights on."
  e.g. "After the memory broke through, the threat felt immediate and physical — not something that had happened, but something that was still happening."
- Memory → Negative Appraisals: The vignette says memories are followed by a conviction that his life was ruined, but does not clearly state that the memory leads to negative appraisals in causal form.
  e.g. "After the image broke through again, she caught herself thinking: if this keeps happening, there must be something deeply wrong with me."
  e.g. "The memory surfaced in the middle of a meeting and she spent the rest of the day convinced that everyone around her could see how broken she was."
  e.g. "Each time the flashback came, the thought that followed it was always the same — that she had let this happen, and that it said something permanent about who she was."
- Memory → Triggers: The vignette does not clearly state that memories themselves generate triggers.
  e.g. "After the memory had surfaced, even the most ordinary things — a kettle whistling, a door slamming — felt like warnings she couldn't afford to ignore."
  e.g. "The intrusive image left her scanning every room she entered, cataloguing exits, tracking faces, unable to switch off."
  e.g. "Because the memory came back so vividly, she began to see threads of it everywhere: in strangers' faces, in certain times of day, in the quality of winter light."
- Threat → Memory: The vignette says feeling threatened increases guarding, but does not clearly state that threat drives the memory/intrusion process.
  e.g. "Walking home on high alert, she passed a doorway and the memory was simply there — pulled out of her by the adrenaline, fully formed."
  e.g. "The persistent sense of danger kept her close to the event in her mind, as if she needed to keep reviewing it to stay one step ahead of whatever came next."
  e.g. "On nights when the threat felt highest, the memory was hardest to keep at bay — it would surface in the dark, vivid and unwelcome."
- Threat → Triggers: The vignette shows feeling unsafe and on guard, but does not clearly state that threat causes triggers to become activated.
  e.g. "Already running on threat, she found that almost anything could tip into a warning — a van parked at an odd angle, a light left on that shouldn't have been."
  e.g. "The background hum of danger she carried everywhere made ordinary cues feel like messages — each one confirming what her body already believed."
  e.g. "Living at that pitch of alertness, she found the world had become dense with reminders she couldn't stop reading."
